answer: Node2vec uses a biased second-order random walk controlled by parameters p (return) and q (in-out). Setting q small (below 1) makes walks more outward-looking, so they behave more like depth-first exploration that moves away from the source. Setting q large (above 1) keeps walks close to the start node, which is BFS-like sampling: the walk stays within the immediate neighborhood of the source, sampling nodes at small distances (e.g., neighbors of neighbors). BFS-style sampling therefore captures structural equivalence, where nodes play similar roles (hubs, bridges, peripheral nodes) and share similar local neighborhood structure. Because the BFS-style walk does not extend far from the source, it does not directly capture homophily, which is the tendency of nearby, densely connected nodes to belong to the same community. Homophily-based community detection is instead favored by DFS-style sampling (small q, meaning larger q-to-p ratio tradeoffs aside), which explores farther into the network and so reaches nodes in the same tightly connected community. So the premise is partly inverted: BFS-style sampling helps with structural roles and local neighborhood similarity, while DFS-style exploration of larger parts of the network is what supports inferring communities based on homophily. Node2vec's p and q let one interpolate between the two behaviors.
